info.title: The Primer API
info.description: The Primer — an AI-generated living storybook and lifelong learning companion for children aged 3-7.

get.description: Returns 200 while the API process is serving requests.

post.description:
Records the child's interaction with a beat and returns **202** immediately; the consequence arrives on the stream (`streamUrl`), not in this response (§18.6).

It answers before anything is generated on purpose. The tap has to be acknowledged on screen within about 100ms (§14.7), and the beat that reacts to it takes seconds — so the row is written here and the generation is started on a worker, which is usually finished by the time the client has reopened the stream.

Idempotent per beat: a double-tap records one choice and the first one stands (`recorded: false` on the second). Sent for **every** interaction, including a beat that only asked the child to carry on — `latencyMs`, `retries` and `assisted` are wellbeing and difficulty signals we want for all of them.

There is no wrong answer to reject: nothing here is checked against the beat's `expected`, and no request to this endpoint can fail the child (§8.5).
post.summary: Submit what the child just did

post.description:
Marks the adventure `completed` (or `abandoned`, for `reason: exit`) and finalises the `PlaySession` with its duration and why it stopped.

Idempotent: an adventure that is already finished is returned unchanged, so the child tapping 'all done' and the page unloading cannot disagree about when the sitting ended.

Until this is called the adventure stays `in_progress` and `POST /children/{id}/adventures` keeps rejoining it, which is what makes a reload land back in the same story rather than paying for a new one.
post.summary: Close the adventure and the sitting

post.description:
Exchange email + password for an access token and a refresh cookie.

`TokenViewBase` already sets `permission_classes = ()` and
`authentication_classes = ()`, which is what a credential endpoint needs;
re-stating them here would only invite someone to "tidy" them into the
project defaults and lock the login page behind a login.
End the session: blacklist the refresh token and delete its cookie.

Rotate the session, using the cookie as the credential.

With `ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS` + `BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION` a *new* refresh
token is issued and the presented one is blacklisted, so the cookie must be
replaced on every call — which `move_to_cookie` does, in the same place it
strips the token from the body.

The token is read from the cookie and **only** from the cookie: accepting a
body as well would leave the old, script-readable path open forever, and a
client that still worked without the cookie is a client that never had to stop
storing the token.

Unauthenticated by inheritance, as in `LoginView` — the refresh token *is* the
credential. `SameSite=Lax` on the cookie is what stops that from being a CSRF
hole; see `apps.accounts.cookies`.

**Its own throttle scope, not `auth`.** This endpoint is called once per page
load, automatically, by every client that has ever been signed in; login is
called by a human, rarely. While they shared one 30/hour budget, a morning of
reloads spent it, `LoginView` then answered 429 to a perfectly correct
password, and — because a failed refresh reads as "your session is over" — the
client had already signed the parent out and sent them to the form that was
refusing them. See `SessionRefreshThrottle`.
post.summary: Rotate the session using the refresh cookie

401.description: No refresh cookie, or it is no longer valid.

get.description:
Narrow a viewset's collection routes to the requesting parent.

`parent_lookup` is the ORM path from the model to the owning parent —
`"parent"` for `Child`, `"child__parent"` for anything hanging off a child.

Detail routes deliberately resolve against the *unscoped* queryset so that
`IsParentOwner` is the thing that rejects them, with a 403. Filtering them
too would give 404 and hide the existence of the row — marginally better
against enumeration, but it would also make an ownership bug indistinguish-
able from a deleted row in the logs, and it is not what the API promises.
Object IDs are UUIDs, so there is nothing here to enumerate.

post.description: Requires an active consent record; returns 403 without one.

Returns the child's in-progress adventure if they have one (**200**), and otherwise generates and persists a story plan and returns the new adventure (**201**). Either way the body carries the SSE URL that streams the beats.

It is idempotent on purpose: a client that has lost the adventure id — a hard refresh, a remount, a second device — must rejoin the same story rather than pay for a new one. A child gets a new adventure once the current one is no longer `in_progress`.

The first beat is generated inside the stream, not here, so the client can open the stream and start the companion's thinking animation immediately.

The stream itself is not in this schema: it is a raw `text/event-stream` endpoint (`GET /api/v1/adventures/{id}/stream`) rather than a DRF view. Its frames are documented in `apps/story/streaming.py`.

get.description:
**200** with the same body as `POST /adventures` when the child has an `in_progress` adventure, **204** when they do not.

This is what the child surface calls on mount: it resumes a story across a reload without the possibility of starting one, so a client bug can cost a request but never a generation.
get.summary: The adventure this child is in the middle of

post.description: Returns immediately with the companion's identity. The reference portrait, canonical expressions and spoken greeting are generated on a worker; poll this endpoint and watch `assets_ready`.

get.description:
The day-two payoff (§4.5). For a child with memories this is generated fresh: the companion greets them by name and refers to one specific thing they did — something they named, chose, counted or loved — before opening today's adventure.

For a brand-new child, and for any failure on the generated path, it returns the fixed first-meeting hello (§4.3) with the audio already attached to the companion. `kind` says which one you are holding; a client must never have to infer that from the text.

It costs a language call and a voice call, so it is throttled like a write. `audio_url` may be null — the scene is designed to work in silence, and a child is never shown that anything is missing.
get.summary: What the companion says when this child arrives

post.description:
Record verifiable parental consent (§13.7).

Create-only on purpose: consent is an audit trail, so a change of mind is a
new record (or a revocation), never an edit of the old one.

get.description: The signed-in parent and their children.

AccessToken.description:
What login and refresh return: the access token, and nothing else.

The refresh half of the pair travels in a cookie the client cannot read, so
this really is the whole body — see `apps.accounts.views`.

AdventureCompanion.description:
The companion, reduced to what the story client needs up front (§18.4).

`voiceId` so the client can pre-warm audio; `name` so the loading scene can
say who is thinking. Nothing else — the portrait and expressions are already
on the companion endpoint.

AdventureEnd.description: The state the adventure was left in.

reason.description:
`completed` when the child reached the warm close, `exit` when they left before it. A wellbeing signal for the parent report, kept separate from whether the story finished.

* `completed` - completed
* `exit` - exit

AdventureStartRequestRequest.description:
The optional client hints on `POST /adventures` (§18.4).

Validated but still not read. Day 11 personalised the world and it did so from
the interest graph and the world map (§11.7, §8.3) rather than from anything the
client says — a device hint is the one input to personalisation that nobody
verified. What is left for this field is mood and time of day, which are real
and are not today's. Declared so a client can send it from the start, and so a
malformed `context` is rejected now rather than on the day we begin reading it.

The field is built in `get_fields` rather than declared as a class attribute
because §18.4 names it `context`, and a class attribute by that name shadows
`Serializer.context` — the request/view dictionary every serializer relies on.
The wire name is what the spec fixes; where the field object lives is ours.

AdventureWorld.description:
Where this adventure happens, as the child's screen needs it (§8.3, §15.1).

Three fields and each one has exactly one consumer. `key` is the palette: it is
put on `data-world` and the stylesheet does the rest, which is why it is a
registry key (`story.worlds`) rather than a display name — a world the CSS has
never heard of renders as the default theme and the child's screen and their
story quietly disagree about where they are. `name` and `place` are for the
grown-up in the room and for the accessibility layer; nothing on the child's
screen is read to them.

Arrival.description:
The greeting a child gets *this visit* (§4.5). Read-only, never stored.

Distinct from `GreetingSerializer` above, which is §4.3's fixed imprint hello
carried on the companion row. This one is decided per arrival and can be either
kind, which is why `kind` is on the wire: the client renders "welcome back" and
"hello for the first time" as different scenes, and it must not have to infer
which it is holding by pattern-matching the text.

`remembered` is the memory the greeting refers to, verbatim. It is sent so the
scene can *show* what the companion is remembering alongside saying it, and
because a greeting that claims to remember something is a claim a parent is
entitled to check (§12.6). Empty on the first-meeting path, where there is
nothing yet to remember.

recorded.description: False when this beat had already been answered and the first answer stands.

streamUrl.description: Reopen this to receive the consequence beat.

ChoiceRequestRequest.description:
What the child's tap sends back (§18.6).

Every field but `beatId` and `choiceKey` is a *signal*, not an answer. §18.6
names `latencyMs` and `retries`; `assisted` joins them because the companion
scaffolding is the thing that distinguishes "found it easy" from "got there
with help", and `apps.learning` reads all three as evidence (§10.4). They are
recorded on every interaction, including a tap that only means "carry on", so
the evidence is not silently missing for the beats that asked something simple.

Nothing here is validated against the beat's `expected`. There is no wrong
answer to check against (§8.5), so `choiceKey` is accepted as sent and the
consequence is written warmly from whatever arrived.

beatId.description: The beat the child was on.

choiceKey.description: The option the child picked. `continue` for a beat that only asked them to carry on.

value.description: What the child actually answered, when the beat asked for one.

latencyMs.description: How long from the beat being ready to the tap.

retries.description: Attempts before this one. Never a score — a difficulty signal.

assisted.description: Whether the companion scaffolded the answer (§8.5).

CompanionCatalog.description: The picker's options (§14.5). Read-only, and the same list the API validates against.

personality_preset.description:
Catalogue key; expands into the stored personality sheet (§9.2).

* `warm_guide` - warm_guide
* `brave_spark` - brave_spark
* `calm_anchor` - calm_anchor
* `curious_helper` - curious_helper

ConsentRecord.description:
Records one verifiable-consent grant.

`parent`, `ip` and `granted_at` are all server-set: a consent record whose
evidence the client could dictate is not evidence.

child_ref.description: Optional child this grant is scoped to. Usually omitted — consent precedes the child.

Me.description: The parent as the client sees them. No permission or staff flags leak out.

PaletteColors.description:
The resolved palette.

Declared field by field rather than left as free JSON so the generated
TypeScript client knows a swatch has a `primary` — and so the catalogue keys
arrive in the picker as unions of literals rather than bare strings, which
is what makes an invalid choice a build error instead of a 400.

SignupResponse.description:
Response shape for signup — documented for the generated TS client.

No `refresh` field, deliberately. The refresh token leaves as an `httpOnly`
cookie (`apps.accounts.cookies`); declaring it here would put it back in the
generated client's type and invite someone to store it.
